catalog_quote: [Rehg 1993:29, quoted verbatim in Zukoff 2021 sec. 2.1 ex. (4)] High pitch occurs on the penultimate mora, while primary stress is on the final mora; secondary stress occurs on alternate preceding morae (Rehg 1993:29). ... Final consonants are non-moraic, while medial coda consonants are moraic. [Kennedy 2002 sec. 2] Medial coda consonants are moraic, whereas final consonants are not ... According to Rehg (1993), primary stress falls on the last mora, and secondary stress strictly on preceding alternate moras. The form du-duup would thus comprise two feet, as in (d)-(duúp). ... a motive for a bimoraic prefix can be found in the stress system, which assigns stress to alternating moraic segments. Table (7) shows how the stress rule applies to each of the different kinds of reduplicated forms ... (Stress-bearing nasals are capitalized). (7) ... pàa.pá duN.du.né dùu.dùu.pék riì.ri.àa.lá ..…
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same work — Kennedy 2002 (WCCFL 21, pp. 222-235); Glottolog 674022 lists the volume editors Mikkelsen & Potts as authors (Cascadilla contents page saved as evidence). The article is held and its stress passage (sec. 2, table 7) is verbatim as in the catalog: primary stress on the last mora, secondary on alternate preceding moras (reporting Rehg 1993). Beyond the items, this search of works with stress in the title downloaded two open sources: Kozasa 2005 (UH dissertation, chair Rehg; ScholarSpace 10125/11699), the only acoustic study of Pohnpeian prosody — silent on position, says Pohnpeian is 'not a pitch accent language' and refers to 'the stress assignment system that the language used to have' (p. 169); and Doane & Ray 1894 (RSNSW), whose sec. 4 'Accent' (p. 424) says Ponape follows the Hawaiian 'law' of mostly penultimate accent — a 19th-century impression that matches Rehg's penultimate high pitch rather than his final-mora stress. Kennedy 2003 (held by the project) re-read: Rehg 1993 restricts moras to vowels and glides and puts primary stress on the last mora of a phrase; moraic stress-bearing nasals are Kennedy's extension citing an unlocatable 'Rehg 2003'. The deciding source Rehg 1993 (OLSP 24:25-46, p. 29) remains unread: HathiTrust search-only (mdp.39015032909148, uva.x002229287), archive.org lending-restricted, no DOI — priority high; PRG 1981 ch. 2 is paywalled (10.1515/9780824844257-003) — priority medium. Nothing read today contradicts the final-mora coding from a modern first-hand source; the best first-hand statement read is Rehg 1986:206 (final vowel of the surface base carries primary stress), which already backs the record. Suggested record additions: caution lines (no acoustic correlate; 'not a pitch accent language'; Zukoff's fieldwork hedge; 19th-century penultimate impressions) and domain = phrase per Kennedy 2003:76 pending Rehg 1993. all lookups went through Crossref, OpenAlex, archive.org, HathiTrust, ScholarSpace and Cascadilla directly.

It is the only first-hand statement of position read in this search of works with stress in the title; nothing downloaded today (Kozasa 2005, Doane & Ray 1894) states a position from first-hand modern observation. Kozasa 2005 (Rehg's own student, an acoustic study) adds that Pohnpeian is 'not a pitch accent language' and speaks of 'the stress assignment system that the language used to have' (p. 169), reinforcing Kennedy 2003's 'apparent stressless' caveat.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes on all copies we hold (Kennedy 2002 sec. 2 and table 7; Zukoff 2021 ex. 4 quoting Rehg 1993:29 verbatim; Rehg 1986:206, 162, 249-250). The classification (primary stress on the final mora = final syllable, secondary on alternate preceding moras, CVV/CVN heavy) faithfully renders Rehg 1993 as transmitted, and Rehg is the authority on Pohnpeian; no instrumental study or competing modern description was found, and WALS/StressTyp-type databases do not code the language. So nothing suggests the final-mora coding is wrong. It is 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced' because the deciding work (Rehg 1993, 22 pp.) and the reference grammar's phonology chapter (PRG 1981 ch. 2) are not yet obtained; the record reaches Rehg 1993 through a handout and a WCCFL paper. sources.citation: Kozasa, Tomoko. 2005. An acoustic and perceptual investigation of vowel length in Japanese and Pohnpeian. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (chair: Kenneth L. Rehg). [extra; found via ScholarSpace; downloaded now]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 52: 'Very few acoustic investigations have been done on Pohnpeian prosody.' p. 127: 'Since Pohnpeian is not a pitch-accent language, I expected that speakers would not use a pitch fall to mark vowel length.' p. 134: 'There was no indication that the Pohnpeian speakers used F0 cues. This was not surprising, as Pohnpeian is not a pitch-accent language.' p. 169: 'The origin of long vowels, at least in nouns, in Pohnpeian is partly related to the stress assignment system that the language used to have.' p. 22: 'Meter in Pohnpeian oral literature is also based on mora count (Fischer, 1959), which supports the proposal that the minimal rhythmic unit in Pohnpeian is the mora (Rehg 1993).'
sources.note: The only instrumental study of Pohnpeian prosody located. It never states a stress position; it measures vowel duration/F0, finds no F0 cue use, calls Pohnpeian 'not a pitch accent language', treats the mora as the rhythmic unit (following Rehg 1993), and refers to the stress-assignment system as one the language 'used to have'. Adds weight to the caution that synchronic Pohnpeian stress is an abstract/rhythmic construct rather than an observed prominence; does not contradict the final-mora position.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: § 4. Accent. The tone syllable of most Hawaiian words is the penultimate. To this there are a few exceptions. In some the tone falls on the ultimate, in others on the ante-penultimate. Suffixed particles possess great power in attracting towards them the accent. This is also the simple law of the Ponape tongue in its accentuation.
sources.locator: sec. 4 'Accent', p. 424 (djvu the text layer); also p. 425 on 'la' (lines 600-603) and the superlative 'heavy accent' (line 1221)
sources.note: A 19th-century missionary statement (by analogy with Hawaiian) that Ponapean accent is mostly penultimate with suffixed particles attracting the accent. Formally at odds with the final-mora coding, but consistent with Rehg 1993's 'high pitch on the penultimate mora' (an untrained ear would hear the pitch peak) and with Gulick 1880's 'accented on the first' for disyllables. Historical curiosity; not a basis for reclassification.
